# Thresholds

I have been thinking about doorways lately, and about how much of life happens in the moment of passing through them.

A doorway is a strange piece of architecture. It is, strictly speaking, an absence: a hole cut in a wall so that we can be somewhere else. Yet almost every culture has treated it as more than a hole. The Romans gave the threshold its own god, Janus, who looked both ways at once. Japanese homes mark the *genkan*, the small sunken entryway where shoes come off, as a border between the dirty world and the clean one. In many traditions the groom carries the bride over the threshold, and in others it is bad luck to step on it. We seem to know, without being told, that something happens at the edge of a room that does not happen in the middle of one.

What happens, I think, is that we become briefly unfinished. In the middle of a room, you are who you are in that room: the person at the desk, the person cooking, the person asleep. At the door you are between roles. You have stopped being one thing and have not yet begun being another. Anyone who has walked into a kitchen and forgotten why knows this. Psychologists even have a name for it, the "doorway effect," in which passing through a door makes the mind file away what it was just holding. The old room's thoughts stay in the old room. The brain treats the wall as a chapter break.

I find this oddly comforting. It suggests that the forgetting is not a malfunction but a kind of housekeeping. The mind is trying to be useful by clearing the stage for a new scene. It only feels like failure because we were attached to the old scene's props.

---

There are other thresholds that aren't made of wood and hinges. The minute before a difficult conversation. The last page of a book, just before you close it and become someone who has read it. The moment on a diving board when you have decided but not yet jumped. Dawn and dusk, which are not exactly day or night, and which almost every poet has been unable to leave alone. The word "twilight" has done more work in literature than most of the nouns around it.

What these moments share is a peculiar quality of attention. Standing in a real doorway, even for a second, you notice things: the draft, the change in light, the smell of the next room. Thresholds sharpen perception because they present two worlds for comparison. In the middle of a state, we stop noticing it. A person who has lived in the same city for twenty years no longer sees its skyline. But arrive by train after a long absence and the skyline is suddenly enormous and specific. Contrast is how the senses work. We detect edges, not expanses.

This may be why travel feels so alive, and why it fades. The first day in a new country is all threshold. Every sign is a puzzle and every meal an event. By the third week you have a favorite café and the country has begun to dissolve into ordinary life. The place has not gotten less interesting. You have simply moved from the doorway into the room.

---

I sometimes wonder whether the trick to a good life is learning to stay a little bit in the doorway. I do not mean literally, since nobody can live in a hallway, though some of us try. I mean keeping the doorway's kind of attention alive within the rooms. Looking at your own street as if you had just arrived. Hearing a friend's voice as if after a long absence, which, in the end, is always true, because every conversation is closer to the last one than we like to admit.

There is a discipline in this, and it is not the same as novelty-seeking. Chasing new experiences is just running from one doorway to the next and never settling anywhere. The harder and more rewarding thing is to bring the freshness of arrival to what is already familiar. Some traditions of meditation aim at exactly this. Beginner's mind, they call it, the willingness to see the cup of tea as though nobody had ever explained a cup of tea to you. It sounds precious until you actually try it, and then it turns out to be difficult and slightly startling. The tea is warmer than you remembered. The steam does something interesting. Ordinary life, examined from its edge, turns out to be full of detail.

---

Thresholds have a shadow side, too. They are where hesitation lives. Everyone has stood at a door they did not want to open: the office of a boss, a hospital room, a house that used to be home. The physical act of turning a handle can feel disproportionately enormous compared with the actual muscle involved. I think this is because we understand, in our bodies, that some doors only swing one way. Once you are through, the room behind you becomes the past, and no amount of turning around will make it the present again.

And yet the alternative, never going through, is its own kind of loss. A life spent hovering in the entryway, keeping every option open, is a life in which nothing happens. The point of a door is that it leads somewhere. The dignity of a threshold comes precisely from the fact that you do eventually cross it.

There is a small courage in the crossing. It doesn't need to be dramatic. Most of the time it is just the ordinary courage of saying yes, or sending the email, or walking into a room where you don't know anyone and deciding to be someone who introduces herself. But if you look closely, every large life is made of these small crossings, stacked end to end like rooms in a long house.

---

I like to imagine that house. Its hallways are narrow and its doors are of every kind: heavy oak, sliding paper, screen doors that slap shut behind you on summer afternoons. Some rooms are bright and some are dim. Some you were glad to leave, and some you would go back to if you could. Behind you the doors have closed, but they are not gone. They stay where they are, attached to their walls, still swinging on their hinges in the memory of the person who walked through them.

And ahead there is always at least one more door, slightly ajar, with a strip of light along the floor. I do not know what is in the next room. Neither do you. That is the whole secret of thresholds, and the reason they feel the way they do: half fear, half appetite, entirely alive.

Turn the handle. See what the light is doing.
